gloss: fearing too much and too readily, and having too little confidence, in the face of danger
gloss_modern: This means fearing danger excessively and losing confidence quickly, so one shrinks from dangers that should be faced.
reasoning: Cowardice is the deficiency of courage: the person fears dangers too much and too readily and lacks confidence when facing them. Today this is simply a person who shrinks from danger and loses nerve.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: feeling fear and confidence in the right measure when facing danger, and standing firm for a worthy end
gloss_modern: This means facing danger with fear and confidence in due measure, standing firm for a worthy cause.
reasoning: The courageous person feels fear and confidence in the right measure when facing danger and stands firm for a worthy end. Today we call this person brave or courageous.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: having too much confidence: rushing at danger with no proper sense of the risk
gloss_modern: This means charging into danger with too much confidence, heedless of the real risks involved.
reasoning: Rashness is the excess of courage: the person has too much confidence and charges at danger without a proper sense of the risk. Today this is someone who acts recklessly and heedlessly.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: taking too little pleasure in food, drink and sex; a type Aristotle says is rarely met
gloss_modern: This means taking too little delight in food, drink and sex, so bodily pleasures barely move one at all.
reasoning: Insensibility is the deficiency of temperance: the person takes too little pleasure in food, drink and sex, so bodily appetites barely stir them. Aristotle notes this type is rare, and today we would call such a person joyless or passionless about the body.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: enjoying the pleasures of the body in the right measure, at the right times, without being ruled by them
gloss_modern: This means enjoying bodily pleasures in due measure and at proper times, never letting appetite rule one's choices.
reasoning: The temperate person enjoys bodily pleasures in the right measure and at the right times without being ruled by them. Today we call this person temperate, moderate or self-controlled.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: pursuing the pleasures of food, drink and sex to excess and being pained when they are missing
gloss_modern: This means chasing food, drink and sex to excess, and becoming distressed whenever these pleasures are absent.
reasoning: Self-indulgence is the excess of temperance: the person pursues food, drink and sex beyond measure and is pained when they are withheld. Today this is someone who gives in to appetites without restraint.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: giving too little and taking too much where money is concerned
gloss_modern: This means giving too little and grabbing too much with money, guarding wealth at others' expense.
reasoning: Meanness is the deficiency of liberality: the person gives too little and takes too much where money is concerned. Today this is a person who hoards money and begrudges spending it.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: giving and taking money in the right measure, to the right people, with pleasure
gloss_modern: This means giving and taking money in proper amounts, to the right people, and taking pleasure in doing so.
reasoning: The liberal person gives and takes money in the right measure, to the right people, and with pleasure. Today we call this person generous or open-handed.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: giving and spending money far too freely, wasting one's substance
gloss_modern: This means spending and giving so freely that one squanders one's own wealth, with no thought for the cost.
reasoning: Prodigality is the excess of liberality: the person gives and spends money far too freely and wastes their own substance. Today this is someone who squanders money recklessly.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: spending too little on great public occasions, spoiling the effect to save a little
gloss_modern: This means skimping on grand public occasions to save a little, thereby ruining the splendor the occasion needed.
reasoning: Niggardliness is the deficiency of magnificence: the person spends too little on great public occasions, spoiling their effect to save a little. Today this is a penny-pincher who cheapens grand occasions.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: spending large sums fittingly and with taste on great occasions and public works
gloss_modern: This means spending large sums fittingly and tastefully on great occasions and public works, producing true grandeur.
reasoning: The magnificent person spends large sums fittingly and with taste on great occasions and public works. Today we call this person magnificent, munificent or splendid in giving.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: spending lavishly on display where it is not fitting, to show off one's wealth
gloss_modern: This means spending lavishly on display where it is out of place, merely to advertise one's wealth to others.
reasoning: Vulgarity here is the excess of magnificence: the person spends lavishly on display where it is out of place, to show off wealth. Today this is someone who flaunts money in tasteless ways.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: thinking oneself worthy of less than one deserves, and so not claiming one's due
gloss_modern: This means underrating oneself, believing one deserves less than one does, and so failing to claim what is owed.
reasoning: Undue humility is the deficiency of magnanimity: the person thinks themselves worthy of less than they deserve and so fails to claim their due. Today this is a self-belittling, spiritless person.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: thinking oneself worthy of great things and being worthy of them
gloss_modern: This means judging oneself worthy of great honors and truly deserving them, neither inflating nor shrinking one's own worth.
reasoning: The magnanimous person thinks themselves worthy of great things and truly is worthy of them. Today we call this person magnanimous or high-minded.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: thinking oneself worthy of great things without being worthy of them
gloss_modern: This means thinking oneself worthy of great honors without the merit to back it, and so puffing up one's standing.
reasoning: Empty vanity is the excess of magnanimity: the person thinks themselves worthy of great things without being worthy of them. Today this is a conceited, boastful person.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: caring too little for honor, even for the honor that would be fitting
gloss_modern: This means caring so little for honor that one declines even the recognition one fairly deserves.
reasoning: Unambitiousness is the deficiency of proper ambition: the person cares too little for honor, even the honor that would fittingly come to them. Today this is someone who is indifferent to recognition and achievement.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: desiring honor as one should and from the right sources; a mean Aristotle says has no name
gloss_modern: This means wanting honor as one should, from right sources, aiming high without grasping at praise.
reasoning: The person with proper ambition desires honor as one should and from the right sources, a mean Aristotle said had no name. Today we would call this person rightly ambitious, aspiring to honor in a fitting way.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: desiring honor more than is right, and from the wrong sources
gloss_modern: This means craving honor beyond what is right and seeking it from unworthy sources.
reasoning: Ambition is the excess of proper ambition: the person desires honor more than is right and from the wrong sources. Today this is someone who craves status and approval too much.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: not getting angry even when anger is called for, and putting up with insult
gloss_modern: This means failing to get angry even when anger is called for, meekly swallowing insults that should provoke a response.
reasoning: Inirascibility is the deficiency of good temper: the person fails to get angry even when anger is called for and puts up with insult. Today this is a spineless, passive person.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: being angry at the right things, with the right people, to the right degree and for the right length of time
gloss_modern: This means getting angry at the right things, toward the right people, to the right degree, and for the right length of time.
reasoning: The good-tempered person is angry at the right things, with the right people, to the right degree and for the right length of time. Today we call this person good-tempered or even-tempered.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: getting angry quickly, too often and too much, at the wrong things
gloss_modern: This means flaring into anger quickly, often, and intensely, even at things that do not warrant it.
reasoning: Irascibility is the excess of good temper: a person flares up at the wrong things, too quickly and too often. Today we call this person hot-tempered.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: understating or disclaiming one's own merits and achievements
gloss_modern: This means habitually downplaying your real merits and achievements, even when they clearly deserve recognition.
reasoning: Mock modesty is the deficiency of truthfulness: a person understates or disowns their real merits and achievements. Today this person is falsely modest, pretending to humility while really withholding the truth about themselves.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: presenting oneself, in word and in life, as neither more nor less than one is
gloss_modern: This means presenting yourself accurately in word and deed, claiming neither more nor less than you actually are.
reasoning: Truthfulness is the mean in which a person presents themselves exactly as they are, neither inflating nor deflating. Today we call this person truthful and honest.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: claiming merits and achievements one does not have, or more of them than one has
gloss_modern: This means claiming achievements you do not have, or exaggerating the ones you do, to impress others.
reasoning: Boastfulness is the excess of truthfulness: a person claims merits they lack or inflates the ones they have. Today this is a boastful, vainglorious person.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: making no jokes and taking offense at those who do
gloss_modern: This means making no jokes yourself and resenting anyone who does, which leaves company stiff and dull.
reasoning: Boorishness is the deficiency of ready wit: a person makes no jokes and resents those who do. Today we call such a person churlish and humorless, a surly, dull presence in company.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: joking tastefully and in the right measure in relaxed company
gloss_modern: This means joking well and in proportion, amusing company without crudeness or hurting anyone's feelings.
reasoning: Ready wit is the mean of joking tastefully and in measure, amusing others without crudeness. Today we call this person witty, with tact in the way they joke.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: trying to raise a laugh at any cost, with no regard for decency or for the feelings of the target
gloss_modern: This means chasing laughs at any cost, with no concern for decency or for whoever the joke wounds.
reasoning: Buffoonery is the excess of ready wit: a person will say anything for a laugh, regardless of decency or of who is hurt. Today we call this person buffoonish or clownish.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: opposing everything and caring nothing for the pain one causes in company
gloss_modern: This means opposing whatever others say and not caring how much discomfort your disagreement causes around you.
reasoning: Quarrelsomeness is the deficiency of friendliness: a person opposes everything and does not care how much pain this causes. Today we call this person cantankerous and contrary.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: being pleasant in company as one should, approving and objecting in the right measure
gloss_modern: This means being pleasant company, agreeing and objecting in measure without flattering or needlessly causing offense.
reasoning: Friendliness is the mean of being pleasant company, approving and objecting in measure. Today we call this person amiable and friendly.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: praising everything and never opposing, so as to give no pain; done for gain it is flattery
gloss_modern: This means praising everything, never disagreeing, and flattering people to avoid displeasure or to win advantage.
reasoning: Obsequiousness is the excess of friendliness: a person praises everything and never opposes, avoiding all displeasure, and for gain it becomes flattery. Today we call this person obsequious or sycophantic.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: feeling no shame at all, even at disgraceful acts
gloss_modern: This means feeling no shame at all, even when committing disgraceful acts, and being unbothered by one's own disgrace.
reasoning: Shamelessness is the deficiency of modesty: a person feels no shame at all, even for disgraceful acts. Today we call this person shameless and brazen.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: feeling shame in the right measure at what is disgraceful
gloss_modern: This means feeling proper shame at disgraceful conduct, in measure, neither indifferent to disgrace nor easily embarrassed.
reasoning: Modesty is the mean of feeling proper shame at disgraceful conduct, in measure. Today we call this person modest and decorous.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: being ashamed of everything, too easily and too much
gloss_modern: This means being ashamed of nearly everything, too readily and too intensely, so that embarrassment governs ordinary conduct.
reasoning: Bashfulness is the excess of modesty: a person is ashamed of nearly everything, too easily and too much. Today we call this person bashful or easily embarrassed.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: falling so short of being pained at others' undeserved good fortune that one rejoices at their ill fortune
gloss_modern: This means being glad when others suffer misfortune, and taking pleasure in their troubles rather than being pained by unearned good fortune.
reasoning: Spite is the deficiency of righteous indignation: a person is so far from pained by others' undeserved good fortune that they rejoice in their misfortune. Today we call this person spiteful and malicious.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: being pained at good fortune that is undeserved
gloss_modern: This means resenting only the undeserved good fortune of others, feeling pain at injustice in proportion to its wrong.
reasoning: Righteous indignation is the mean of being pained at undeserved good fortune. Today we call this person righteously indignant, resenting unearned success in proportion.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: being pained at all good fortune of others, deserved or not
gloss_modern: This means resenting others' good fortune whether or not they deserve it, so that their successes pain you as a matter of course.
reasoning: Envy is the excess of righteous indignation: a person is pained by all good fortune of others, deserved or not. Today we call this person envious and begrudging.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: living with no regard for anyone else, taking no account of what others want
gloss_modern: This means acting with no regard for anyone else, ignoring what others want as if their wishes did not matter.
reasoning: Self-will is the deficiency of dignity: a person lives with no regard for others and ignores what they want. Today we call this person self-willed and headstrong.
source: Eudemian Ethics II.3 (Rackham); the fuller account in III.7

gloss: keeping a proper measure of regard for others, neither ignoring them nor living only to please them
gloss_modern: This means balancing self-respect with consideration, neither dismissing others nor bending everything to win their approval.
reasoning: Dignity is the mean of keeping proper regard for others without living to please them. Today we call this person dignified and self-respecting.
source: Eudemian Ethics II.3 (Rackham); the fuller account in III.7

gloss: adjusting everything to what others want, living to please them
gloss_modern: This means shaping everything you do around others' wishes, living to please them and giving up your own judgment.
reasoning: Subservience is the excess of dignity: a person adjusts everything to others' wishes and lives only to please them. Today we call this person subservient or servile.
source: Eudemian Ethics II.3 (Rackham); the fuller account in III.7

gloss: lacking the shrewdness to see how to reach one's ends, and so being easily taken in
gloss_modern: This means lacking the shrewdness to see how to reach your aims, so that others easily take advantage of you.
reasoning: Simpleness is the deficiency of practical wisdom: a person lacks the shrewdness to find the means to their ends and is easily taken in. Today we call this person naive and gullible.
source: Eudemian Ethics II.3 (Rackham); the fuller account in III.7

gloss: deliberating well about what is good for a human life and how to achieve it
gloss_modern: This means weighing well what is good for your life and finding the right way to reach it.
reasoning: Practical wisdom is the mean of sound judgment about what is good for a whole human life and how to reach it. The person who has it deliberates carefully and acts well in ordinary affairs, which is what we now call prudence.
source: Eudemian Ethics II.3 (Rackham); the fuller account in III.7

gloss: being clever at reaching any end at all, good or bad; cunning without scruple
gloss_modern: This means turning sharp wits toward any aim at all, honest or corrupt, with no qualms about method.
reasoning: Rascality is the excess of practical wisdom: skill at achieving any end whatever, good or bad, with no moral restraint. Today this is a person whose cleverness serves whatever aim they hold, without scruple.
source: Eudemian Ethics II.3 (Rackham); the fuller account in III.7

gloss: hiding one's real thoughts and plans behind friendly words, pretending to know or intend nothing
gloss_modern: This means hiding your true aims behind friendly words while pretending you intend nothing.
reasoning: The dissembler hides real thoughts and plans behind friendly words and pretends to intend nothing. Today we would call this person duplicitous, a deceiver whose warmth is a cover.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 1 (Jebb 1870: "The Dissembler")

gloss: praising and fawning on someone in order to profit by it
gloss_modern: This means heaping praise and servile attention on someone in order to profit by it.
reasoning: The flatterer praises and fawns on others to gain some advantage. Today this is the sycophant, someone who buys favor with empty praise.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 2 (Jebb 1870: "The Flatterer")

gloss: pouring out long, rambling talk on trivial matters to anyone who cannot escape
gloss_modern: This means pouring out endless talk on trivial matters at anyone trapped within earshot.
reasoning: The garrulous person pours out long, rambling talk about trivia on anyone who cannot get away. Today this is a long-winded bore who corners listeners.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 3 (Jebb 1870: "The Garrulous Man")

gloss: ignorance of social manners: coarse, uncouth and loud in company
gloss_modern: This means behaving coarsely and loudly in company, ignorant of or indifferent to good manners.
reasoning: The boor is ignorant of social manners and behaves coarsely, uncouthly and loudly in company. Today we say boorish or uncouth for this person.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 4 (Jebb 1870: "The Boor")

gloss: trying to please everyone and to give no offense, agreeing with all sides
gloss_modern: This means agreeing with everyone and avoiding any offense, even at the cost of honesty.
reasoning: The complaisant person is so eager to please and avoid offense that he agrees with every side and gives way to all. Today this is the people-pleaser who sacrifices candor to keep everyone happy.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 5 (Jebb 1870: "The Complaisant Man")

gloss: loss of all sense of shame or scruple in word and deed, ready to do anything disreputable
gloss_modern: This means acting and speaking with no sense of shame, ready for anything that reflects badly on you.
reasoning: This person has lost all sense of shame or scruple in word and deed and will do anything disreputable. Today we call such a person brazen, unashamed of disgraceful conduct.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 6 (Jebb 1870: "The Reckless Man")

gloss: talking incessantly, unable to hold one's tongue, interrupting and holding forth
gloss_modern: This means talking nonstop, interrupting others and holding forth without letting anyone else speak.
reasoning: The loquacious person talks incessantly, cannot hold his tongue, interrupts others and holds forth. Today this is a chatterbox who dominates conversation.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 7 (Jebb 1870: "The Talker")

gloss: inventing news and rumors and passing them on as fact
gloss_modern: This means inventing news and rumors and spreading them around as established fact.
reasoning: The rumor-monger invents news and gossip and passes it off as fact. Today this is a rumormonger who spreads fabrications as truth.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 8 (Jebb 1870: "The Newsmaker")

gloss: disregarding one's reputation for the sake of petty gain, such as cheating creditors or sponging
gloss_modern: This means throwing away your good name for petty gains, like cheating creditors or sponging off others.
reasoning: The shameless person discards his reputation for petty gain, such as cheating creditors or living off others. Today we call this person shameless or disreputable, someone who cares little for good name.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 9 (Jebb 1870: "The Shameless Man")

gloss: excessive economy over tiny sums, counting every coin
gloss_modern: This means being obsessively frugal over trifling sums, counting every coin even when it is petty.
reasoning: The penurious person is excessively economical over tiny sums and counts every coin. Today this is a stingy, penny-pinching miser.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 10 (Jebb 1870: "The Penurious Man")

gloss: open, offensive indecency and coarse jesting in public
gloss_modern: This means openly joking coarsely and indecently in public, offending anyone who is within hearing.
reasoning: The gross person openly indulges in offensive indecency and coarse jesting in public. Today we would call such a person vulgar, obscene or crude in company.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 11 (Jebb 1870: "The Gross Man")

gloss: choosing the wrong time for everything, to the annoyance of those one deals with
gloss_modern: This means consistently choosing the wrong moment for things, annoying the people you deal with.
reasoning: The unseasonable person chooses the wrong time for everything and irritates those he deals with. Today this is a tactless person whose timing is always off.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 12 (Jebb 1870: "The Unseasonable Man")

gloss: well-meant but overeager readiness to help, promise and interfere
gloss_modern: This means offering help and promises too eagerly, interfering in others' affairs without being asked.
reasoning: The officious person is eagerly ready to help, promise and interfere, though his zeal is overdone. Today this is a meddler who intrudes into others' affairs unasked.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 13 (Jebb 1870: "The Officious Man")

gloss: slowness of mind in word and act; forgetting, missing the point
gloss_modern: This means being slow to grasp things, forgetting easily, and missing the point in speech and action.
reasoning: Stupidity here is slowness of mind in word and act, with forgetting and missing the point. Today we say the person is obtuse or slow-witted.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 14 (Jebb 1870: "The Stupid Man")

gloss: rudeness and ungraciousness in speech, refusing courtesy
gloss_modern: This means speaking gruffly and grudgingly, refusing ordinary courtesy to those you deal with.
reasoning: The surly person is rude and ungracious in speech and refuses ordinary courtesy. Today surly describes a gruff, sullen and disobliging person.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 15 (Jebb 1870: "The Surly Man")

gloss: cowardice toward the supernatural, fussing over omens, rites and pollution
gloss_modern: This means fretting anxiously over omens, rites and ritual purity out of fear of the supernatural.
reasoning: The superstitious person is cowardly before the supernatural and frets over omens, rites and ritual pollution. Today this is someone governed by irrational fear of the unseen and of omens.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 16 (Jebb 1870: "The Superstitious Man")

gloss: unreasonable fault-finding with one's lot, complaining even of favors
gloss_modern: This means finding fault with your circumstances unreasonably, complaining even when you are favored.
reasoning: The grumbler finds unreasonable fault with his lot and complains even about favors he receives. Today this is a querulous, discontented complainer.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 17 (Jebb 1870: "The Grumbler")

gloss: presuming dishonesty in everyone, checking up on all
gloss_modern: This means assuming everyone is dishonest and constantly checking up on people to catch them out.
reasoning: The distrustful person presumes everyone dishonest and checks up on all. Today we call this person suspicious or mistrustful, believing the worst of others by default.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 18 (Jebb 1870: "The Distrustful Man")

gloss: neglect of one's person to the point of disgusting others
gloss_modern: This means neglecting personal hygiene and appearance so thoroughly that others find one disgusting.
reasoning: The vice is neglecting one's person so badly that others are disgusted. Today this is a person who is repulsively dirty and unkempt, with no regard for how they affect those around them.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 19 (Jebb 1870: "The Offensive Man")

gloss: behavior that causes annoyance without doing harm: tactless remarks, embarrassing stories
gloss_modern: This means causing annoyance through clumsy remarks and embarrassing anecdotes, though without intending real harm.
reasoning: This is a habit of causing annoyance without real harm, through clumsy remarks and embarrassing anecdotes. Today we would call this person tactless and irritating, someone who is hard to be around socially.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 20 (Jebb 1870: "The Unpleasant Man")

gloss: an ignoble desire for distinction, seeking credit and display in trifles
gloss_modern: This means chasing public honor and credit over trifles, craving display and recognition beyond their worth.
reasoning: The vice is an ignoble craving for honor, pursued through trifles and displays. Today this person is vainglorious, always angling for applause and credit over small things.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 21 (Jebb 1870: "The Man of Petty Ambition")

gloss: lack of generosity where honor or expense is concerned, avoiding any outlay
gloss_modern: This means refusing to spend even when honor or decency requires generosity, avoiding every outlay.
reasoning: This vice is an unwillingness to spend, even where honor or decency calls for generosity. Today this is a stingy, miserly person who grudges every expense.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 22 (Jebb 1870: "The Mean Man")

gloss: pretending to advantages, wealth or connections one does not have
gloss_modern: This means claiming wealth, status or connections one lacks, and bragging about them to impress.
reasoning: The vice is pretending to wealth, standing, or connections one does not possess. Today this is a boastful pretender who puts on airs to impress others.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 23 (Jebb 1870: "The Boastful Man")

gloss: contempt for everyone except oneself, refusing to give anyone their due
gloss_modern: This means looking down on everyone else, withholding their due and treating oneself as the only one who counts.
reasoning: This is contempt for others combined with a refusal to grant them their due. Today we call this person haughty and contemptuous, someone who treats everyone else as beneath them.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 24 (Jebb 1870: "The Arrogant Man")

gloss: giving way to fear, seeing danger everywhere and slipping away from it
gloss_modern: This means yielding to fear, seeing danger everywhere and slipping away from any risk.
reasoning: The vice is yielding to fear and seeing danger everywhere. Today this is a craven, timid person who flees any risk.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 25 (Jebb 1870: "The Coward")

gloss: love of authority, greedy for power and gain, scorning the common people
gloss_modern: This means craving authority and profit while looking down on ordinary people as beneath consideration.
reasoning: This is a love of authority combined with greed for power and profit, and contempt for ordinary people. Today this is a power-hungry elitist who sees rank as a right and the common people as beneath them.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 26 (Jebb 1870: "The Oligarch")

gloss: taking up in old age the pursuits of youth, and making a fool of oneself
gloss_modern: This means an elderly person who takes up youthful pursuits and makes a fool of themselves doing so.
reasoning: The vice is an old person taking up the pursuits of youth and embarrassing themselves. Today we call this person childish in old age, playing at things that suit someone much younger.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 27 (Jebb 1870: "The Late-Learner")

gloss: a habit of saying malicious and damaging things about others
gloss_modern: This means habitually speaking maliciously and damagingly about others, often behind their backs.
reasoning: This is a habit of speaking maliciously and damagingly about others. Today this is a slanderous, backbiting gossip who harms reputations behind people's backs.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 28 (Jebb 1870: "The Evil-Speaker")

gloss: a fondness for bad people, consorting with and defending rogues
gloss_modern: This means consorting with and defending bad people, showing a taste for rogues.
reasoning: The vice is a fondness for bad people, keeping their company and defending them. Today this person is fond of scoundrels, cultivating and shielding crooks.

gloss: eagerness for base gain, profiting shabbily at the expense of others
gloss_modern: This means eagerly pursuing base gain, profiting shabbily at others' expense.
reasoning: This vice is an eagerness for base gain that profits at others' expense. Today this is a greedy, grasping person who takes advantage of others for money.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 30 (Jebb 1870: "The Avaricious Man")

gloss: an inflated sense of one's own worth, putting oneself above others

gloss: a modest estimate of one's own importance, putting oneself no higher than others

gloss: an insatiable desire for wealth and possessions
gloss_modern: This means endlessly craving wealth and possessions, never content with what one already has.

source: the seven deadly sins (Gregory I's list, as later tradition names it)

gloss: free and willing giving; charity toward those in need
gloss_modern: This means giving freely and willingly, especially to those in need, without grudging.

source: the seven contrary virtues (after Prudentius, Psychomachia)

gloss: an intense, uncontrolled desire for sexual pleasure
gloss_modern: This means being driven by intense, unrestrained sexual desire that one fails to control.

source: the seven deadly sins (Gregory I's list, as later tradition names it)

gloss: restraint and purity in sexual conduct
gloss_modern: This means keeping sexual conduct restrained and pure, holding desire within proper bounds.
reasoning: Chastity is restraint and purity in sexual conduct. Today this is a chaste person who keeps sexual desire within proper limits.
source: the seven contrary virtues (after Prudentius, Psychomachia)

gloss: resentment of others' goods, success or qualities, wishing them for oneself
gloss_modern: This means begrudging others' goods, success or qualities and wanting them for oneself.

source: the seven deadly sins (Gregory I's list, as later tradition names it)

gloss: good will toward others, rejoicing in their good
gloss_modern: This means wishing others well and taking genuine pleasure in their good fortune.
reasoning: Kindness here is good will toward others, rejoicing in their good. Today this is a benevolent person who wishes others well and is glad of their success.

gloss: overindulgence in food and drink
gloss_modern: This means eating and drinking to excess, indulging appetite far beyond what is good for one's health or sense.
reasoning: Gluttony is the sin of overindulging in food and drink, eating and drinking past what the body or good sense needs. A person given to it today is a glutton, someone who cannot stop at enough.
source: the seven deadly sins (Gregory I's list, as later tradition names it)

gloss: moderation in food and drink
gloss_modern: This means eating and drinking in moderation, never letting appetite overrule what is sensible and healthy.
reasoning: This is the virtue opposed to gluttony: restraint in eating and drinking. A person who has it is abstemious, enjoying food and drink without letting appetite take over.
source: the seven contrary virtues (after Prudentius, Psychomachia)

gloss: uncontrolled anger, hatred and the wish for revenge
gloss_modern: This means letting anger and hatred run unchecked, nursing thoughts of revenge against those who have crossed them.
reasoning: Wrath is uncontrolled anger, hatred and a desire for revenge. The person given to it is wrathful, letting rage and grudges rule them.
source: the seven deadly sins (Gregory I's list, as later tradition names it)

gloss: bearing provocation and delay calmly, without resentment
gloss_modern: This means enduring provocation and delay calmly, holding no grudge and not lashing out at those who annoy them.
reasoning: Patience is the virtue opposed to wrath: bearing provocation and delay calmly without resentment. Today a person with it is simply patient, slow to anger and free of grudges.
source: the seven contrary virtues (after Prudentius, Psychomachia)

gloss: laziness and indifference about one's duties and the good
gloss_modern: This means being lazy and indifferent toward one's obligations and toward what is good, neglecting what one should do.
reasoning: Sloth is laziness and indifference toward one's duties and toward the good. The person given to it is idle and careless about what they ought to do, which is a slothful person.
source: the seven deadly sins (Gregory I's list, as later tradition names it)

gloss: careful, steady effort in one's work and duties
gloss_modern: This means working steadily and carefully at one's tasks and duties, applying sustained effort rather than letting things slide.
reasoning: Diligence is the virtue opposed to sloth: careful, steady effort in one's work and duties. A person who has it is conscientious and hardworking.
source: the seven contrary virtues (after Prudentius, Psychomachia)

gloss: the practical wisdom to judge what is right to do in the circumstances
gloss_modern: This means judging well what is right to do in the circumstances, weighing situations sensibly before acting on them.
reasoning: Prudence is practical wisdom, the ability to judge what is right to do in particular circumstances. A person who has it is sensible and sound in their decisions.
source: the four cardinal virtues (Plato, Republic IV; Ambrose)

gloss: giving each person their due, in word and deed
gloss_modern: This means giving each person their due, in what one says and what one does, and treating others fairly.
reasoning: Justice is giving each person their due in word and deed. A person who has it is fair-minded and upright in dealing with others.
source: the four cardinal virtues (Plato, Republic IV; Ambrose)

gloss: courage and endurance in the face of danger, pain and hardship
gloss_modern: This means facing danger, pain and hardship steadily, enduring them without letting fear take over one's conduct.
reasoning: Fortitude is courage and endurance in the face of danger, pain and hardship. A person who has it stands firm when things are hard and does not flee from fear.
source: the four cardinal virtues (Plato, Republic IV; Ambrose)

gloss: self-restraint and moderation in every pleasure
gloss_modern: This means restraining oneself and keeping moderation in every pleasure, not only in food and drink.
reasoning: As a cardinal virtue, temperance is self-restraint and moderation in every pleasure, not only eating and drinking. A person who has it keeps their desires in check across the board.
source: the four cardinal virtues (Plato, Republic IV; Ambrose)

gloss: firm belief in God and in what has been revealed
gloss_modern: This means holding firm belief in God and in what has been revealed, and living by that trust.
reasoning: Faith here is firm belief in God and in what has been revealed. A person who has it is devout, and their belief shapes how they live.

gloss: confident expectation of the good to come, and trust in its promise
gloss_modern: This means expecting good things to come with assurance, and trusting that what has been promised will arrive.
reasoning: Hope is confident expectation of the good to come and trust in its promise. A person who has it looks forward to good outcomes with assurance.
source: the three theological virtues (1 Corinthians 13)

gloss: love of God and of one's neighbor, shown in self-giving
gloss_modern: This means loving God and one's neighbor, and showing that love through generous self-giving toward others.
reasoning: Charity here is love of God and of one's neighbor, shown through self-giving. A person who has it is loving and generous toward others, not merely giving money.
source: the three theological virtues (1 Corinthians 13)

gloss: thinking of new and productive ways to do things

reasoning: Creativity is the strength of thinking up new and productive ways of doing things. A person who has it is inventive and original in solving problems.

gloss: creativity used too little, or not at all, where it would serve

gloss: taking an interest in experience for its own sake, exploring and discovering
gloss_modern: This means taking genuine interest in experience for its own sake, exploring and discovering new things out of pure interest.
reasoning: Curiosity is taking interest in experience for its own sake, exploring and discovering. A person who has it is eager to learn and to see how things work.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: curiosity used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means showing little interest in learning or exploring, leaving things unexamined even where inquiry would help.
reasoning: This is curiosity used too little, where it would serve. The person is incurious, showing little interest in learning or exploring anything beyond what is required.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: curiosity used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means poking into others' affairs and asking intrusive questions beyond what is useful or welcome.
reasoning: This is curiosity used past the point where it serves, becoming intrusion into others' affairs. The person is nosy, prying into matters that are none of their business.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: thinking things through and examining them from all sides; not jumping to conclusions
gloss_modern: This means weighing matters carefully from every side and refusing to leap to conclusions before examining the evidence.
reasoning: Judgment is the strength of thinking things through and examining them from all sides without jumping to conclusions. A person who has it is judicious and discerning.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: judgment used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means acting or deciding without weighing evidence or considering the alternatives, even when careful thought would clearly help.
reasoning: Unreflectiveness is judgment left unused, so the person decides or acts without weighing evidence or considering alternatives. Today this is someone who reacts without thinking things through.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: judgment used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means assuming bad motives in everyone and dismissing sincere effort, so that nothing and no one is taken at face value.
reasoning: Cynicism is judgment pushed past its use, so the person doubts every motive and claim and assumes the worst. Today this is someone who distrusts everything and everyone by reflex.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: mastering new skills, topics and bodies of knowledge
gloss_modern: This means continually seeking out new skills and subjects and enjoying the work of mastering them for their own sake.
reasoning: A love of learning is a steady drive to master new skills, topics and bodies of knowledge. The person who has it is a lifelong learner who enjoys studying for its own sake.

gloss: love of learning used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means being satisfied with what one already knows and never troubling to acquire new skills or understanding.
reasoning: Complacency is a love of learning left unused, so the person is satisfied with what they already know and makes no effort to learn more. Today this is someone who has stopped growing intellectually.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: love of learning used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means lecturing others on every subject and presuming to be an expert on matters one has only glanced at.
reasoning: Know-it-all-ism is learning displayed too much, so the person lectures others and pretends to expertise on everything. Today this is a smug, pedantic show-off.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: being able to give wise counsel; seeing the world in ways that make sense to oneself and others
gloss_modern: This means offering sound counsel and seeing situations clearly, in ways that make sense to oneself and to those one advises.
reasoning: Perspective is the capacity to give wise counsel and to see the world in ways that make sense to oneself and others. The person who has it is a sound adviser whose view of events is clear and widely trusted.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: perspective used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means judging matters by their surface and offering others little insight or sound counsel on what really matters.
reasoning: Shallowness is perspective left unused, so the person judges by surface appearances and offers little real insight. Today this is someone who never looks beneath the surface of things.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: perspective used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means imposing one's own view on others, lecturing and dictating until they stop listening or disagreeing.
reasoning: Overbearing is perspective pushed too far, so the person forces their own view on others and will not hear theirs. Today this is someone who dominates conversations and lectures people into agreement.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: not shrinking from threat, challenge, difficulty or pain; speaking up for what is right
gloss_modern: This means facing threat, difficulty or pain without flinching, and speaking up for what is right even when it costs.
reasoning: Bravery is not shrinking from threat, difficulty or pain and speaking up for what is right. The person who has it faces danger and hardship steadily and stands up for others when it costs them.

gloss: bravery used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means shrinking from danger, challenge or discomfort, and staying silent even when one ought to speak up.
reasoning: Cowardice is bravery left unused, so the person shrinks from danger, challenge or discomfort and keeps quiet when they should speak. Today this is someone who flinches from risk and stays silent in the face of wrong.

gloss: bravery used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means charging into danger heedlessly and taking risks that serve no purpose and that a sensible person would avoid.
reasoning: Foolhardiness is bravery pushed past sense, so the person runs into danger heedlessly for no good purpose. Today this is someone who takes pointless, reckless risks.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: finishing what one starts; persisting in the face of obstacles
gloss_modern: This means finishing what one starts and pressing on steadily when obstacles and setbacks arise.
reasoning: Perseverance is finishing what one starts and persisting through obstacles. The person who has it sticks to long tasks and keeps going when things get hard.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: perseverance used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means abandoning projects at the first setback and giving up as soon as obstacles appear.
reasoning: Fragility is perseverance left unused, so the person drops projects at the first setback. Today this is someone who gives up easily and never sees things through.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: perseverance used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means pursuing one goal past all reason, unable to let go even when the effort is futile or doing harm.
reasoning: Obsessiveness is perseverance pushed past reason, so the person cannot let go of a goal even when it is futile or harmful. Today this is someone fixated and unable to stop.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: speaking the truth and presenting oneself genuinely
gloss_modern: This means speaking the truth and presenting oneself as one genuinely is, without pretense or concealment.
reasoning: Honesty is speaking the truth and presenting oneself genuinely. The person who has it is truthful and transparent, and what they show of themselves is what they are.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: honesty used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means presenting a false self to others, pretending to feelings and opinions one does not actually hold.
reasoning: Phoniness is honesty left unused, so the person presents a false self and pretends to feelings and opinions they do not hold. Today this is someone who is fake and two-faced.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: honesty used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means blurting out every hard truth and moralizing about it, sure of one's own rectitude and indifferent to the hurt it causes.
reasoning: Righteousness is honesty pushed past good sense, so the person blurts out every hard truth and moralizes about it. Today this is someone self-righteous and tactless, indifferent to how much their candor hurts.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: approaching life with excitement and energy
gloss_modern: This means approaching life with excitement and energy, throwing oneself eagerly into work, play and people.
reasoning: Zest is approaching life with excitement and energy. The person who has it throws themselves eagerly into what they do and brings enthusiasm to daily life.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: zest used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
